```{r}
#| label: web-font

# Open Sans, from Google Fonts, so that tables look the same in every browser
gdtools::register_gfont("Open Sans", subset = c("latin", "latin-ext", "greek"))
knitr::knit_meta_add(list(gdtools::gfontHtmlDependency("Open Sans", subset = c("latin", "latin-ext", "greek"))))
```

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| cache: false
library(apa7)
library(dplyr)
library(flextable)
library(ftExtra)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(correlation)
apa7_defaults(font_family = "Open Sans", line_spacing = 1.5)
```

```{r loading}
<<setup>>
```

Correlation matrices look simple enough...until you try to make one by hand in MS Word. The `apa_cor` function can remove most of the tedium by formatting most of what can automated, and any finishing touches can be added with a styling function.

The examples use the `epi.bfi` data set from the psychTools package [@revellePsychToolsToolsAccompany2019], which has personality, depression, and anxiety scores for 231 participants in studies at Northwestern University's Personality, Motivation, and Cognition Laboratory. Openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism are Big Five scale scores, and depression is the Beck Depression Inventory score. 

```{r}
#| label: data
d_personality <- psychTools::epi.bfi |>
  select(
    Openness = bfopen,
    Conscientiousness = bfcon,
    Extraversion = bfext,
    Agreeablness = bfagree,
    Neuroticism = bfneur,
    Depression = bdi
  )
```

`apa_cor` returns a table that is displayed in APA style in documents, with significant correlations starred. In the console, it is an ordinary tibble.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cor
#| tbl-cap: Correlations Among Personality and Depression
#| message: false
tbl_cor <- apa_cor(d_personality)
tbl_cor
```

`apa_note` writes the table's note. The text is in markdown, and it does not start with "*Note*." because apaquarto adds that:

```{r}
#| label: note
apa_note(tbl_cor)
```

With [apaquarto](https://wjschne.github.io/apaquarto/), use `apa_note` in the `apa-note` chunk option (e.g., `#| apa-note: !expr apa7::apa_note(tbl_cor)`), with the table made in an earlier chunk. Without apaquarto, `apa_flextable(note = TRUE)` puts the note below the table, as in the rest of this article:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cor-note
#| tbl-cap: Correlations Among Personality and Depression With a Note
apa_flextable(tbl_cor, note = TRUE)
```

Significant correlations can be bolded instead.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bold
#| tbl-cap: Correlations With Significant Correlations in Bold
#| message: false
d_personality |>
  apa_cor(bold_significant = TRUE) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

```

# Summary functions

You can include any named list of summary functions:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-median-iqr
#| tbl-cap: "Correlations Among Personality and Depression With Medians and Interquartile Ranges"
# Named list of descriptive functions
my_summaries <- list(Mdn = median, "*IQR*" = IQR)

apa_cor(d_personality,
        summary_functions = my_summaries,
        star_significant = FALSE) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```


You can also use a plain vector of descriptive functions from these options: `"IQR", "Interquartile Range", "Kurtosis", "MAD", "Median Absolute Deviation", "M", "Mean", "Med", "Median", "n", "N", "Quantile", "Range", "SD", "Skewness", "Var", "Variance"`

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summaries
#| apa7-width: landscape
#| tbl-cap: "Correlations Among Personality and Depression With Additional Summary Statistics"
my_summaries <- c("n", "M", "SD", "Skewness", "Kurtosis")

apa_cor(d_personality, summary_functions = my_summaries) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

```


# Options

`apa_cor` decides what the table shows:

* `alpha` *p*-value thresholds for one, two, and three stars (with `bold_significant = TRUE`, only the first is used). Default: `c(.05, .01, .001)`
* `digits` Number of decimal places. Default: `2`
* `bold_significant` Whether to bold significant correlations instead of starring them. Default:  `FALSE`
* `star_significant` Whether to star significant correlations. Default: `TRUE`
* `significance_note` Whether the note explains the stars (or bolding). The note does not explain them if no correlations are significant. Default:  `TRUE`
* `keep_empty_star_columns` Whether correlation columns without significant correlations keep their star columns, so that all correlation columns have the same width. Default: `TRUE`

`apa_flextable` decides how it looks:

* `note` `TRUE` for the note from `apa_note`, or a markdown-formatted note of your own. Default: `NULL` (no note)
* `font_family` Font family (typeface). Default: `Times New Roman`
* `font_size` Font size (in points). Default: `12`
* `text_color` Text color. Default: `black`
* `border_color` Table border color. Default: `black`
* `border_width` Table border width (in points). Default: `0.5`
* `line_spacing` Text line spacing. Default: `2`
* `table_width` Width of the table (e.g., `.5` for half the page width). Default: the full width of the page

The defaults of the styling options can be set for all tables with `apa7_defaults`. For example,

```{r}
#| label: tbl-altstyle
#| tbl-cap: Correlations With Alternative Styling

d_personality |>
  apa_cor(
    alpha = 0.001,
    digits = 2,
    bold_significant = TRUE,
    significance_note = TRUE,
    summary_functions = my_summaries
  ) |>
  apa_flextable(
    note = TRUE,
    font_family = "Arial",
    font_size = 10,
    text_color = "darkred",
    border_color = "royalblue4",
    border_width = 1,
    line_spacing = 2
  )
```

To remove summary statistics entirely, set `summary_functions` to `NA` or `NULL`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-nosummary
#| tbl-cap: Correlations Without Summary Statistics
apa_cor(d_personality, summary_functions = NA) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

# Customization

The styling options of `apa_flextable` are minimal, but flextable allows for all kinds of customization. Just place whatever code from flextable you want after `apa_flextable`. Here I set the width to 50%, and I place a footnote in a specific cell in the table body.


```{r}
#| label: tbl-altflextable
#| tbl-cap: Correlations Styled With flextable Functions
apa_cor(d_personality) |>
  apa_flextable(table_width = .5) |>
  flextable::footnote(
    i = 2,
    j = "Variable",
    value = flextable::as_paragraph("This is a footnote."),
    part = "body"
  )

```

# Changing the tibble

Because `apa_cor` returns a tibble, you can change it with dplyr and tidyr functions before passing it to `apa_flextable` (or to a table function from another package). Here we add a row title.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-tibble
#| tbl-cap: Correlations With a Row Title
apa_cor(d_personality) |>
  mutate(apa7listcolumn = str_trim(apa7listcolumn)) |>
  unite(col = Variable, 
        apa7listcolumn, 
        Variable, 
        sep = "&thinsp;") |>
  add_row(Variable = "Row title", .before = 1) |>
  apa_flextable(no_format_columns = "Variable") |>
  padding(i = 2:7,
          j = 1,
          padding.left = 15)
```

# Other Kinds of Correlations

`apa_cor` computes the correlations with `correlation::correlation` from the [correlation](https://easystats.github.io/correlation/) package: by default, Pearson correlations with unadjusted *p*-values. Depression scores are skewed, as the skewness in the summary statistics above shows, so rank correlations are a reasonable alternative. The `method` argument chooses the kind of correlation. For example, Spearman rank correlations:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-spearman
#| tbl-cap: Spearman Rank Correlations Among Personality and  Depression
#| message: false
apa_cor(d_personality, method = "spearman") |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

The note says what kind of correlations are shown. Other options for `method` include:

| Option        | Correlation                    |
|:--------------|:-------------------------------|
| `pearson`     | Pearson's Correlation (default)|
| `spearman`    | Spearman's Rank Correlation    |
| `kendall`     | Kendall's Rank Correlation     |
| `biserial`    | Biserial Correlation           |
| `polychoric`  | Polychoric Correlation         |
| `tetrachoric` | Tetrachoric Correlation        |
| `biweight`    | Biweight midcorrelation        |
| `distance`    | Distance Correlation           |
| `percentage`  | Percentage Bend Correlation    |
| `blomqvist`   | Blomqvist's coefficient        |
| `hoeffding`   | Hoeffding's D                  |
| `gamma`       | Gamma Correlation             |
| `gaussian`    | for Gaussian Rank correlation  | 
| `shepherd`    | for Shepherd's Pi correlation  |

To adjust the *p*-values (and so the stars) for multiple comparisons, use `p_adjust` (e.g., `p_adjust = "holm"`), and the note says how they were adjusted. Partial correlations, each controlling for the other variables in the table, need only `partial = TRUE`:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-partial
#| tbl-cap: Partial Correlations Among Personality and Depression
#| message: false
apa_cor(d_personality, partial = TRUE) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

Partial correlations can differ considerably from ordinary correlations. With zero-order correlations, openness and extraversion correlate at .27, but once other personality variables are held constant, the partial correlation between them is close to zero.

Other arguments of `correlation::correlation` (e.g., `robust = TRUE`, `winsorize = .2`, or `multilevel = TRUE`) can be given to `apa_cor` as well. Variable names with spaces work for every kind of correlation, because `apa_cor` gives the variables internal names while it computes the correlations. (Called directly, `correlation::correlation` does not accept such names for partial or multilevel correlations.)

The output of `correlation::correlation` can also be given to `apa_cor`:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-correlation-output
#| tbl-cap: Spearman Rank Correlations Computed by the correlation Package
#| message: false
correlation(d_personality, method = "spearman") |>
  apa_cor() |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

Here, `correlation::correlation` adjusted the *p*-values with Holm's method, its default, so the stars are for the adjusted *p*-values, and the note says so. The means and standard deviations come from the data that `correlation::correlation` keeps with its results. Correlations computed by group, between two sets of variables, or with Bayesian methods are not yet supported.
